questions.stem: A developer wants Claude to read, edit, and run tests across the files of a local Git repository from the terminal. Which entry point is the best fit?

options.A: claude.ai chat, pasting the repository files in one at a time by hand each time
options.B: Claude Code, which works directly with your repository in the terminal
options.C: A Claude Project with the whole repository zipped and attached as a knowledge source
options.D: The API, with a custom script the developer writes and maintains

questions.explanationCorrect: Claude Code is the terminal-based entry point built to read, edit, and run code across a repository directly. It is purpose-built for hands-on local codebase work.
questions.explanationDistractor: A Project knowledge source is read-only reference material; it cannot edit files or run tests, so zipping the repo into a Project does not enable the work described.

questions.stem: Your team answers customer questions using the same product FAQ, tone guidelines, and policy documents every day, and you want every chat to start with that context without pasting it each time. Which entry point best fits?

options.A: A brand-new claude.ai chat every time, pasting the FAQ, tone guide, and policy documents in at the start
options.B: Claude Code, with the FAQ and policy documents kept in a repository
options.C: A Claude Project with the FAQ and policies as knowledge and the tone in custom instructions
options.D: The API, embedding all of the documents in every single request

questions.explanationCorrect: Projects let you set durable custom instructions and attach knowledge sources, so every chat in the Project inherits that context automatically. That is ideal for a repeated workflow with shared reference material.
questions.explanationDistractor: Re-pasting the documents into a fresh chat each time is exactly the manual repetition Projects eliminate; it is error-prone and easy to forget.

questions.stem: An engineer needs Claude to classify incoming support tickets automatically inside the company's own application, with no person in the loop. Which entry point is most appropriate?

options.A: The Claude Developer Platform API, called from the application's code
options.B: claude.ai chat, with a staff member manually pasting in each incoming ticket
options.C: A Claude Project shared with the whole support team
options.D: Claude Code running in one of the individual developers' local terminals

questions.explanationCorrect: Programmatic, automated classification inside your own software is what the API is for: the application sends each ticket to Claude and acts on the response with no manual steps.
questions.explanationDistractor: claude.ai chat requires a person to paste each ticket and read each answer, which defeats the goal of automatic, in-app classification.

questions.stem: A marketer wants to brainstorm ten taglines for a campaign and refine the best few in a quick back-and-forth. There is no code, no repeated workflow, and nothing confidential. Which entry point is the simplest appropriate choice?

options.A: The API, driven by a short Python script
options.B: Claude Code, used from the terminal
options.C: A dedicated Claude Project with knowledge sources
options.D: A claude.ai chat conversation

questions.explanationCorrect: For a quick, one-off, conversational task with no code or reusable context, a plain claude.ai chat is the simplest fit; no extra setup is warranted.
questions.explanationDistractor: Creating a Project with knowledge sources is unnecessary overhead for a single throwaway brainstorm that will not be repeated.

questions.stem: You need Claude to work through a complex, multi-step financial analysis that requires careful reasoning, and where subtle mistakes are costly. Speed and cost are secondary. Which model is the best default?

options.A: Claude Haiku 4.5, for the fastest possible response
options.B: Claude Opus 4.8, for the strongest reasoning
options.C: Whichever model happens to be cheapest that day
options.D: Claude Sonnet 5, chosen mainly to minimize latency

questions.explanationCorrect: Opus 4.8 is the most capable model for the hardest, multi-step reasoning. When accuracy on a complex task outweighs speed and cost, it is the right default.
questions.explanationDistractor: Haiku 4.5 is optimized for speed and simple tasks; using it for costly, subtle multi-step reasoning trades away the capability the task demands.

questions.stem: A product feature will summarize thousands of documents per day. Each summary is moderately complex, and you need a strong balance of quality, speed, and cost at scale. Which model is the most appropriate default?

options.A: Claude Opus 4.8 for every request, regardless of the cost
options.B: Claude Haiku 4.5, accepting weaker quality on harder documents
options.C: Claude Sonnet 5, balancing quality and cost at volume
options.D: A model chosen at random per request

questions.explanationCorrect: Sonnet 5 is designed for the balanced, high-volume middle ground: strong quality at a cost and speed that scale to thousands of requests. It fits moderately complex work at volume.
questions.explanationDistractor: Running Opus 4.8 on every request maximizes quality, but its cost and latency are hard to justify across thousands of moderately complex summaries per day.

questions.stem: You need to detect whether each incoming message is written in English or Spanish: a simple, high-volume, latency-sensitive classification. Which model is the best fit?

options.A: Claude Haiku 4.5, the fastest and most economical option
options.B: Claude Opus 4.8, reached for just to be extra safe on accuracy
options.C: Whichever model happens to have the largest available context window
options.D: A separate Opus call per language, then compared side by side

questions.explanationCorrect: Haiku 4.5 is built for simple, fast, high-volume tasks like language detection, delivering low latency and low cost where heavier reasoning is not needed.
questions.explanationDistractor: Reaching for Opus 4.8 "to be safe" on a trivial classification wastes cost and latency without meaningfully improving a task Haiku handles well.

questions.stem: A logic puzzle keeps tripping Claude up because it involves several dependent reasoning steps. Which built-in capability is most directly aimed at improving multi-step reasoning like this?

options.A: Web search, to look the puzzle's answer up on the open internet
options.B: Extended (adaptive) thinking, which lets Claude reason through steps before answering
options.C: File uploads, to attach the puzzle to the chat as a PDF document
options.D: Artifacts, to render the finished answer neatly in its own dedicated side panel for later review

questions.explanationCorrect: Extended (adaptive) thinking gives Claude room to reason through intermediate steps before committing to an answer, which directly helps on multi-step problems.
questions.explanationDistractor: Artifacts only change how output is displayed in a side panel; they do nothing to improve the underlying reasoning on a multi-step problem.

questions.stem: You ask Claude about a regulation that changed last week, after the model's training cutoff. Which feature should you enable to get an accurate, current answer?

options.A: Extended thinking, so Claude can reason harder about the new regulation
options.B: Artifacts, used to format the final answer nicely in a side panel
options.C: Web search, so Claude can retrieve up-to-date information
options.D: A larger maximum output length setting

questions.explanationCorrect: Web search lets Claude retrieve current information from the internet, which is essential for facts that changed after its training cutoff. Reasoning alone cannot recover knowledge the model never had.
questions.explanationDistractor: Extended thinking helps Claude reason about what it already knows; it cannot conjure facts about an event that postdates its training data.

questions.stem: You are drafting a policy document with Claude and want to see it in a dedicated panel, edit it across turns, and keep a stable version as you refine it. Which feature is designed for this?

options.A: Artifacts, a side panel for substantial, editable content
options.B: Web search, used to gather outside sources for the document
options.C: Extended thinking, to plan out the document's structure first
options.D: Token counting, to measure the document's overall size

questions.explanationCorrect: Artifacts render substantial, self-contained content (like a document or code) in a dedicated, editable side panel you can iterate on across turns, which is exactly this use case.
questions.explanationDistractor: Web search retrieves information; it has nothing to do with displaying and iterating on a document you are co-writing.

questions.stem: A colleague sends you a 40-page PDF contract and asks for a plain-language summary of its key obligations. In claude.ai, what is the most direct way to have Claude work from the actual document?

options.A: Retype the whole contract into the chat box by hand
options.B: Upload the PDF file directly to the conversation
options.C: Describe the contract from memory and let Claude fill the gaps
options.D: Ask Claude to search the web to find the contract

questions.explanationCorrect: claude.ai supports file uploads, including PDFs, so Claude can read the actual document and summarize it accurately rather than working from a paraphrase.
questions.explanationDistractor: Describing the contract from memory strips out the exact terms Claude needs and invites an inaccurate summary of a document Claude never actually saw.

questions.stem: After a long chat that drifted across several unrelated topics, Claude's answers start pulling in irrelevant details from earlier in the conversation. What is the best way to manage this?

options.A: Keep going and just hope the accumulated noise clears on its own
options.B: Repeat your latest question in all capital letters
options.C: Start a new conversation focused only on the current topic
options.D: Switch to a smaller and faster model midway through the long chat

questions.explanationCorrect: Everything earlier in a conversation is context Claude may draw on. When accumulated, unrelated history starts to interfere, a fresh conversation gives Claude a clean, focused context.
questions.explanationDistractor: Switching to a smaller model does not remove the irrelevant conversation history that is actually causing the interference.

questions.stem: You want Claude to answer a specific question about one section of a large report. Which approach gives Claude the most useful context to work with?

options.A: Paste the entire multi-hundred-page report and ask the question at the very end
options.B: Provide the relevant section (or a focused excerpt) and state the specific question
options.C: Ask the question with no context and let Claude infer the report
options.D: Send the question first, then the report separately hours later

questions.explanationCorrect: Giving Claude the relevant section plus a clear, specific question focuses its attention on what matters. Focused, on-point context generally produces better answers than dumping everything or nothing.
questions.explanationDistractor: Dumping hundreds of irrelevant pages buries the pertinent section and can dilute Claude's attention, making a precise answer harder rather than easier.

questions.stem: You find yourself pasting the same brand style guide into a new chat several times a week to keep Claude's writing on-brand. What is the better long-term setup?

options.A: Keep pasting the brand style guide into each new chat, since it only takes a minute
options.B: Memorize the style guide so you can paraphrase it more quickly
options.C: Create a Project with the style guide as knowledge and the brand voice in custom instructions
options.D: Email the style guide to Claude and ask it to remember for you

questions.explanationCorrect: When the same reference is reused repeatedly, moving it into a Project (knowledge source plus custom instructions) means every chat inherits it automatically: durable, consistent, and no re-pasting.
questions.explanationDistractor: Continuing to paste the guide every time is the manual, error-prone repetition that a Project is designed to eliminate.

questions.stem: A teammate runs every task, even trivial reformatting, on the largest, most expensive model "to be safe." What is the most sensible guidance?

options.A: Always default to the largest model, since its extra reasoning capability is never actually wasted
options.B: Match the model to the task, using a smaller model for simple work and the largest for hard reasoning
options.C: Always default to the smallest available model to keep the per-task cost as low as possible
options.D: Rotate between the models at random each time so usage is spread evenly across them

questions.explanationCorrect: Model selection is about fit: simple, high-volume tasks run well on Haiku or Sonnet, while Opus is reserved for the hardest reasoning. Matching model to task controls cost and latency without sacrificing needed quality.
questions.explanationDistractor: "Always use the largest model" pays premium cost and latency for trivial work that a smaller model handles just as correctly.

questions.stem: You want Claude to review a draft email the way an experienced communications editor would. Which addition to your prompt most directly sets that up?

options.A: Assign a clear role, like "act as an experienced communications editor," and say what to review
options.B: Simply ask it to "be helpful and thorough" and see what comes back
options.C: Paste the draft email in with no other instructions and simply let Claude decide what to do
options.D: Ask for the longest, most detailed response it can produce

questions.explanationCorrect: Giving Claude a specific role plus a clear task focuses its behavior and standards on the job; an editor's lens produces more targeted feedback than a vague request.
questions.explanationDistractor: "Be helpful and thorough" is too vague to steer the review; it gives Claude no concrete role, criteria, or focus to apply.

questions.stem: Claude keeps returning its answer as flowing paragraphs, but you need a table with three named columns to drop into a report. What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Ask the exact same question over again and simply hope that it comes back formatted as a table
options.B: Switch to a larger, more capable model and simply try the identical request one more time
options.C: Tell Claude to "make it look a bit nicer and more polished" before you paste it into the report
options.D: Explicitly specify the output format: a table with the three exact column names you need

questions.explanationCorrect: Stating the desired output format precisely, a table with named columns, tells Claude exactly how to structure the response. Being explicit about format is the reliable way to get it.
questions.explanationDistractor: "Make it look nicer" is subjective and unspecified; Claude cannot reliably infer that you want a three-column table from it.

questions.stem: You ask Claude to "write a follow-up message to the client," but its draft misses that the client is upset about a missed deadline. What would most improve the result?

options.A: Ask Claude to work a general, non-specific apology in somewhere near the opening of the message
options.B: Repeat the exact same request again, word for word, and hope that the second draft lands better
options.C: Provide the context: the client's complaint, the missed deadline, and the outcome you want
options.D: Ask Claude to make the message noticeably shorter and more direct in its overall tone and phrasing

questions.explanationCorrect: Claude can only account for facts it is given. Supplying the situation, the client's concern, and your goal lets Claude write a genuinely responsive message instead of a generic one.
questions.explanationDistractor: Repeating the identical request gives Claude no new information, so the draft will keep missing the context it never received.

questions.stem: You need Claude to (1) analyze survey data, (2) draft an executive summary, and (3) create a slide outline. A single prompt asking for all three at once yields shallow results on each. What is the better approach?

options.A: Demand noticeably more detail and depth while still keeping it all in the same all-in-one prompt
options.B: Break the work into sequential steps, doing and reviewing each before moving to the next
options.C: Ask for all three again, but this time request a larger font
options.D: Drop two of the three tasks to simplify the request

questions.explanationCorrect: Decomposing a complex, multi-part request into focused steps lets Claude give each its full attention, and lets you check the output of one step before it feeds the next.
questions.explanationDistractor: Cramming more instructions into the same overloaded prompt keeps Claude splitting attention across three tasks at once, which is why each came out shallow.

questions.stem: An output is not quite right, so in one new attempt you rewrite the role, add three examples, change the format, and swap models all at once. It improves, but you have a problem. What is it?

options.A: Nothing at all is wrong here; changing everything at once is simply the fastest path to a fix
options.B: You should have changed even more of the variables all together within that same single attempt
options.C: The model is now permanently biased by every single thing you tried in your earlier attempt
options.D: You changed too many variables at once, so you cannot tell which change actually helped

questions.explanationCorrect: Diagnostic iteration means changing one variable at a time and observing the effect. Altering many things simultaneously makes the improvement uninterpretable and hard to reproduce.
questions.explanationDistractor: Changing even more at once compounds the problem: you would have zero ability to attribute the result to any specific change.

questions.stem: Your prompts often produce vague, off-target answers. Which single change tends to help the most?

options.A: Making the prompt longer by padding it out with polite filler around the actual request
options.B: Asking Claude to simply "be thorough" and then leaving all of the rest to it
options.C: Being specific about what you want: the exact scope, format, and criteria
options.D: Sending the identical request several more times in a row

questions.explanationCorrect: Specificity is the highest-leverage prompting habit: stating the exact scope, format, and success criteria removes the guesswork that produces vague answers.
questions.explanationDistractor: Telling Claude to "be thorough" adds no concrete direction; it does not tell Claude what to cover or how to shape the answer.

questions.stem: You need every product description formatted in a very specific pattern, and written instructions keep producing near-misses. What most reliably locks in the exact format?

options.A: Provide two or three worked examples of the input and the exact output you want (few-shot)
options.B: Add the word "exactly" to the instruction and then repeat it
options.C: Ask Claude to try harder and be more careful next time
options.D: Make the written instruction paragraph a good deal longer and pack in considerably more detail

questions.explanationCorrect: When a format is hard to convey in words, showing two or three concrete input-to-output examples (few-shot) demonstrates the pattern directly and is more reliable than more prose.
questions.explanationDistractor: Adding emphasis words like "exactly" does not clarify an ambiguous format; Claude still has to guess the pattern you never actually showed it.

questions.stem: Claude keeps misinterpreting how you want a data field transformed, even after you reworded the instruction twice. What is the most effective next move?

options.A: Reword the very same instruction a third time and simply hope that it finally lands
options.B: Tell Claude that it is plainly wrong and then firmly ask it to correct the field
options.C: Switch the output to all capital letters for emphasis
options.D: Show a concrete before-and-after example of the transformation you want

questions.explanationCorrect: When instructions keep being misread, a concrete input-to-output example removes the ambiguity by demonstrating the exact transformation, which is often clearer than any wording.
questions.explanationDistractor: Rewording the instruction a third time is more of the same approach that already failed twice; a demonstration communicates what words could not.

questions.stem: A colleague's prompts are just a one-line task with no other detail, and results are inconsistent. Which set of additions best reflects good prompt structure?

options.A: Much louder wording, plenty of capital letters, and a lot more exclamation points for emphasis
options.B: A clear role, the task, relevant context, the desired output format, and an example or two
options.C: A higher maximum-token setting and a request for the longest answer
options.D: Several unrelated questions bundled together into one message

questions.explanationCorrect: Well-structured prompts typically combine role, a clear task, relevant context, an explicit output format, and examples. Together these remove ambiguity and steer Claude toward the intended result.
questions.explanationDistractor: Bundling several unrelated questions together fragments Claude's focus and makes the prompt harder to answer well, not easier.

questions.stem: You keep telling Claude "don't be so formal," but the tone still misses. Which instruction is likely to work better?

options.A: Describe the tone you do want, warm and conversational like advice to a colleague, with a short example
options.B: Repeat the instruction to "never, ever use any formal words at all" to Claude much more emphatically
options.C: Tell Claude firmly to "stop being so formal" and leave it there
options.D: Ask Claude to simply "be less of everything" from now on

questions.explanationCorrect: Positively describing the target, the tone you do want with an example, gives Claude something concrete to aim at, which steers behavior better than a vague prohibition.
questions.explanationDistractor: "Stop being formal" says what to avoid but not what to do instead, leaving Claude to guess at the tone you actually want.

questions.stem: You want Claude to answer questions using your company's internal policy, which it was never trained on. What is the essential step?

options.A: Simply assume that Claude already has your company's private internal policy memorized in full
options.B: Ask Claude to imagine what the internal policy probably says
options.C: Switch to a bigger model so that it "knows more" about it
options.D: Provide the policy text as context (paste it or attach it) so Claude answers from it

questions.explanationCorrect: Claude has no knowledge of your private, internal documents unless you supply them. Giving it the actual policy text as context is what lets it answer accurately from your source.
questions.explanationDistractor: A bigger model has more general capability but still has never seen your internal policy; capability cannot substitute for the missing document.

questions.stem: A teammate asks Claude to "make this report better" and is frustrated by the results. What advice best addresses the root problem?

options.A: Ask Claude to define what "better" should mean for you
options.B: Run the same request on every model and compare the results
options.C: Tell Claude what "better" means here: clearer structure, shorter, more data-driven, and so on
options.D: Simply accept that Claude cannot ever meaningfully improve written business reports

questions.explanationCorrect: "Better" is subjective; Claude cannot read your mind about which dimension you care about. Naming the specific improvements you want turns an ambiguous ask into an actionable one.
questions.explanationDistractor: Asking Claude to define "better" just outsources your own criteria; it may optimize for a dimension you did not actually care about.

questions.stem: For a straightforward task like "summarize this paragraph in one sentence," Claude already does exactly what you want. When is adding few-shot examples actually worth the effort?

options.A: Always add several worked examples to every single prompt you write, no matter how simple the task is
options.B: Never add examples, since they only end up confusing the model
options.C: When the task has a specific format or edge cases that plain instructions keep getting wrong
options.D: Only when you happen to be using the smallest available model

questions.explanationCorrect: Few-shot examples pay off when a task has a particular format or tricky edge cases that instructions alone do not nail. For simple tasks Claude already handles, the extra examples add little.
questions.explanationDistractor: Adding examples to every prompt regardless of need is wasted effort and token cost when a plain instruction already yields exactly what you want.

questions.stem: Your first prompt gives a decent but too-technical answer for a general audience. What is the most efficient single adjustment to try next?

options.A: Completely rewrite the whole prompt from scratch, making many different changes all at once
options.B: Switch your entry point over from the claude.ai chat interface across to the developer API
options.C: Ask the very same prompt three or four more times and then keep whichever answer reads best
options.D: Add one instruction specifying the audience and reading level, then compare the result

questions.explanationCorrect: Making one targeted change, specifying the audience, and observing the effect is efficient diagnostic iteration: you learn exactly whether that lever fixed the issue.
questions.explanationDistractor: Rewriting everything at once may fix it, but you lose the ability to tell which change mattered, making the next iteration harder.

questions.stem: A prompt reads simply "Write a job description," and the drafts come back generic and unusable. Which elements are most important to add?

options.A: The role, the responsibilities, the required skills, the sections to include, and the tone
options.B: A far more emphatic tone, plenty of bold text, and several extra exclamation points for energy
options.C: A request for the maximum possible length and lots of extra detail
options.D: A firm demand that Claude not make any mistakes this time

questions.explanationCorrect: A generic draft is usually a symptom of a generic prompt. Supplying the specific role, responsibilities, required skills, structure, and tone gives Claude the substance to produce something usable.
questions.explanationDistractor: Demanding that Claude "not make mistakes" provides none of the concrete details, role, skills, or structure, that the draft is actually missing.

questions.stem: Claude's answer includes three specific statistics attributed to named studies. Before you use them in a published report, what should you do?

options.A: Independently verify each statistic, and that the cited studies actually say it
options.B: Trust the statistics, since Claude took care to cite specific, named studies for each one
options.C: Publish the report first and then correct it later on if anyone happens to complain
options.D: Assume any confidently stated number in the answer is reliable

questions.explanationCorrect: Claude can produce fluent, specific-looking citations that are inaccurate or fabricated. For anything you publish, verify each factual claim and citation against the primary source before relying on it.
questions.explanationDistractor: A confident, specific citation is not evidence of accuracy; Claude can state a fabricated source just as fluently as a real one, so trusting it unverified is risky.

questions.stem: An answer is written with total confidence and reads smoothly, with no hedging. What can you conclude about its accuracy?

options.A: Confident, fluent, and polished writing means the answer is almost certainly correct
options.B: Fluency and confidence say nothing about accuracy; it can be confidently wrong
options.C: The complete lack of any hedging in it proves that it was carefully fact-checked
options.D: Smooth, polished writing indicates the model used web search

questions.explanationCorrect: The tone and fluency of an answer are independent of its correctness. Claude can be confidently and articulately wrong, so confidence is not a reliability signal.
questions.explanationDistractor: Absence of hedging is a stylistic feature, not a fact-check; it does not mean the claims were verified against any source.

questions.stem: You ask Claude for case law supporting an argument, and it returns a citation with a court, year, and quote that looks authoritative, but you cannot find the case anywhere. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: The case is genuinely real but simply far too obscure to appear anywhere at all
options.B: Your own search skills are the problem; the citation is surely valid
options.C: Claude may have hallucinated a plausible-looking but nonexistent citation
options.D: The court itself must have quietly pulled the case from every public record somewhere

questions.explanationCorrect: Models can generate citations that look authoritative but do not exist, a hallucination. If a specific, checkable source cannot be found, treat it as unverified rather than assuming it is merely obscure.
questions.explanationDistractor: Assuming the citation must be valid and blaming your search ignores a well-known failure mode: confidently formatted citations that were never real.

questions.stem: Claude drafts what looks like sound guidance on adjusting a patient's medication dosage. What is the responsible way to use this output?

options.A: Follow the dosing guidance directly, since the underlying clinical reasoning looks detailed
options.B: Share it with the patient right away as a definitive answer
options.C: Use it only if it happens to agree with your initial hunch
options.D: Treat it as a draft to be reviewed and approved by a qualified medical professional

questions.explanationCorrect: Medical dosing is high-stakes and potentially irreversible, so it requires human expert verification. Claude's output should be treated as a draft for a qualified professional to review, never a final clinical decision.
questions.explanationDistractor: Following detailed-looking reasoning directly skips the professional judgment that high-stakes medical decisions require; detail is not the same as clinical validation.

questions.stem: Claude generates a database command that will permanently delete every record matching a filter. What should you do before running it?

options.A: Review and verify exactly what it will delete before executing an irreversible action
options.B: Run it immediately to save yourself some time
options.C: Run the command against the live production database first, then check it after
options.D: Assume it is perfectly safe simply because Claude wrote it

questions.explanationCorrect: Irreversible actions demand human verification first. Reviewing precisely what the command affects before executing catches mistakes while they are still reversible.
questions.explanationDistractor: Assuming the command is safe because Claude produced it skips the check that matters most, exactly when the consequences cannot be undone.

questions.stem: You use Claude to screen resumes and notice its shortlist skews heavily toward one demographic. What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Trust the ranked shortlist completely, since the model is objective and neutral by design
options.B: Treat it as a possible bias signal, examine the criteria, and add human review
options.C: Assume the applicant pool itself simply looked that way
options.D: Remove the human reviewers from the process to speed it up

questions.explanationCorrect: AI outputs can reflect and amplify bias. A skewed result is a signal to scrutinize the criteria and keep human oversight, especially for consequential decisions about people.
questions.explanationDistractor: Treating the model as inherently objective ignores that it can reproduce bias; a skewed shortlist warrants investigation, not blind trust.

questions.stem: Claude summarizes a long report and includes a striking claim you do not remember reading. Before quoting that claim, what is the right step?

options.A: Quote the striking claim directly, since summaries are reliable by their very nature
options.B: Rephrase the striking claim so that it ends up sounding a good deal less striking
options.C: Check the claim against the source document to confirm it is actually there
options.D: Delete the entire summary, just to be on the safe side

questions.explanationCorrect: Summaries can introduce claims that are not in the source. Verifying a surprising claim against the original document guards against repeating something Claude inferred or fabricated.
questions.explanationDistractor: Rephrasing a claim to sound less striking does nothing to establish whether it is actually supported by the source.

questions.stem: For which task is it most reasonable to accept Claude's output with only a light check?

options.A: Calculating the exact correct dosage for a patient's prescription
options.B: Drafting the binding wording of a legal contract for signature
options.C: Confirming a specific historical date for a soon-to-be-published article
options.D: Brainstorming a list of possible names for an internal project

questions.explanationCorrect: Verification effort should scale with stakes. A low-stakes, easily reversible, non-factual task like brainstorming internal names carries little risk if a suggestion is imperfect.
questions.explanationDistractor: A binding legal contract is high-stakes and hard to reverse; its wording needs careful human review, not a light check.

questions.stem: You are about to send a client-facing analysis that Claude largely wrote, under your own name. What is the guiding principle?

options.A: You are accountable for it, so validate the facts and reasoning before it goes out
options.B: Claude actually wrote the analysis, so any errors it contains are not your responsibility
options.C: Client-facing work really needs no more care than internal notes
options.D: Send it now, since clients generally expect the occasional error

questions.explanationCorrect: When you put your name on Claude's output, you own its accuracy. Validating the facts and reasoning before it goes out is the core responsibility of using AI in real work.
questions.explanationDistractor: Disclaiming responsibility because "Claude wrote it" does not hold up; the person who sends the work is accountable for it.

questions.stem: Asked for market-size figures, Claude returns very precise numbers such as "$4.37B in 2023" with no source. How should you treat them?

options.A: Use the figures exactly as-is, since their very precision signals that they are reliable
options.B: Treat them as unverified estimates and confirm against a real source before using
options.C: Round the numbers off, which is what makes them accurate
options.D: Assume that Claude just now retrieved them from a live and up-to-date market database

questions.explanationCorrect: Oddly precise figures with no source are a classic hallucination pattern. Precision is not provenance; confirm the numbers against an authoritative source before relying on them.
questions.explanationDistractor: Precision does not signal reliability; a fabricated figure can be stated to the cent just as easily as a rounded one.

questions.stem: A quick way to gauge whether a long Claude answer is trustworthy on a topic you do not know well is to:

options.A: Count up how many separate sources the long answer happens to mention in total
options.B: See whether the entire answer sounds confident all the way through to the end
options.C: Spot-check a few claims you can verify against known facts or sources
options.D: Measure how long the overall response happened to turn out to be in total

questions.explanationCorrect: Spot-checking verifiable claims gives real evidence about accuracy. If the checkable parts are wrong, that is a strong signal to distrust the parts you cannot immediately verify.
questions.explanationDistractor: The number of sources mentioned says nothing about whether those sources are real or support the claims; it is easy to list citations that do not check out.

questions.stem: Claude reviews a vendor contract and flags no issues, and your company is about to sign. What is the responsible next step?

options.A: Sign the contract right away, since Claude reviewed it and flagged nothing at all
options.B: Skip the legal review entirely to save both time and money
options.C: Assume that no flags raised must simply mean there is no real legal risk
options.D: Have a qualified lawyer review it before signing a binding agreement

questions.explanationCorrect: A binding contract is high-stakes and hard to reverse. Claude's review can assist, but a qualified legal professional must verify before you commit; "no flags" is not legal clearance.
questions.explanationDistractor: Treating "Claude found nothing" as proof of no legal risk over-trusts a tool that can miss issues and is not a substitute for professional legal judgment.

questions.stem: A team has used Claude for months with good results and now approves its outputs without any review. What is the main risk?

options.A: Errors will slip through unnoticed precisely because no one is checking anymore
options.B: The model will eventually run out of processing capacity
options.C: Reviewing the outputs was clearly never really necessary here in the first place anyway
options.D: Claude will eventually refuse to answer anything at all without a reviewer present

questions.explanationCorrect: A good track record does not make outputs infallible. Dropping verification entirely means the inevitable errors reach production with nothing to catch them; appropriate review should remain.
questions.explanationDistractor: Concluding review was never necessary misreads past success; the good results likely depended in part on the very checking now being removed.

questions.stem: Claude provides a real, working URL as a citation for a claim. What still needs checking?

options.A: Nothing further; a working link on its own fully validates the claim
options.B: That the linked source actually says what the claim attributes to it
options.C: Only that the link happens to load reasonably quickly in a browser
options.D: Only the linked website's overall visual design and layout

questions.explanationCorrect: A valid link is necessary but not sufficient. Claude may cite a real page that does not actually support the specific claim, so you must confirm the source says what is attributed to it.
questions.explanationDistractor: A link merely loading proves the page exists, not that its content backs the claim it was attached to.

questions.stem: Which output most clearly demands independent human verification before you act on it?

options.A: A short, lighthearted haiku that Claude drafted for a close friend's birthday card
options.B: A list of lighthearted icebreaker questions for a casual internal team meeting
options.C: A suggested set of accent colors and a palette for an internal team slide deck
options.D: A tax-filing figure Claude calculated that you will submit to the authorities

questions.explanationCorrect: Verification scales with stakes and reversibility. A tax figure you will formally submit is high-stakes, factual, and consequential if wrong, so it demands independent verification, unlike creative, low-risk outputs.
questions.explanationDistractor: A haiku for a birthday card is low-stakes and subjective; an error carries no real consequence, so it does not require the same scrutiny.

questions.stem: You are deciding which parts of a monthly reporting process to hand to Claude. Which step is the best candidate to delegate?

options.A: Reformatting the raw numbers into the standard report template, a repeatable and checkable step
options.B: Deciding whether to lay off part of the team based on the numbers
options.C: Choosing the company's confidential, high-level strategic priorities for the entire year
options.D: Signing off on the final figures that will go to the board

questions.explanationCorrect: The best tasks to delegate are well-specified, repeatable, and easy to verify. Reformatting numbers into a template fits all three; the judgment-heavy, accountability-bearing steps stay with a human.
questions.explanationDistractor: Deciding whether to lay off a team is a high-stakes judgment call with human accountability, exactly the kind of step to keep with a person.

questions.stem: Which task should stay with a human rather than being fully delegated to Claude?

options.A: Converting a plain bulleted list into a neatly formatted table
options.B: Making the final call on a sensitive personnel decision
options.C: Drafting an initial first version of routine meeting notes
options.D: Suggesting a few alternative synonyms for a marketing headline

questions.explanationCorrect: Ambiguous, high-stakes decisions that carry human accountability, like sensitive personnel calls, should remain human judgments. Claude can inform them but should not own them.
questions.explanationDistractor: Converting a list to a table is a mechanical, low-risk transformation that is a fine fit for delegation, unlike a consequential personnel decision.

questions.stem: You are presenting a new Claude-assisted workflow to leadership. How should you describe its capabilities?

options.A: Promise leadership that it is fully autonomous and completely error-free, to build their confidence
options.B: Avoid mentioning any of its limitations so that the project gets approved
options.C: Present both the value and the limitations honestly, including where human review is still required
options.D: Claim it will replace the entire team almost immediately

questions.explanationCorrect: Responsible adoption depends on setting accurate expectations. Communicating both the value and the limitations, including where humans stay in the loop, builds durable trust and prevents overreliance.
questions.explanationDistractor: Promising an error-free, fully autonomous system oversells the tool and sets up the project to lose credibility the first time it makes a mistake.

questions.stem: You personally get great results from Claude, but your teammates get inconsistent ones on the same tasks. What best moves the team from "I use Claude" to "our workflow uses Claude"?

options.A: Keep all of your best prompting techniques to yourself and quietly hold them as a personal edge
options.B: Tell your teammates that they simply need to try harder
options.C: Let everyone on the team figure it out on their own
options.D: Capture the working prompts, context, and configuration in a shared setup others can reuse

questions.explanationCorrect: Scaling from individual to team use means turning personal know-how into shared, reusable assets: documented prompts, shared Project instructions, and knowledge, so everyone gets consistent results.
questions.explanationDistractor: Leaving each teammate to figure it out independently reproduces the very inconsistency you are trying to solve; the knowledge stays trapped with one person.

questions.stem: A team wants a first win with Claude. Which process is the best starting candidate?

options.A: A frequent, well-defined, low-risk task with clear inputs and checkable outputs
options.B: The single most ambiguous and highest-stakes decision that the whole team currently faces
options.C: A rare, one-off kind of task that the team will essentially never have to repeat again
options.D: A tangled process that nobody on the team currently understands

questions.explanationCorrect: Good first candidates are frequent, well-defined, and low-risk with verifiable outputs: they deliver clear value, are easy to validate, and build confidence before tackling harder work.
questions.explanationDistractor: Starting with the most ambiguous, high-stakes decision maximizes risk and the chance of a visible failure, undermining early adoption.

questions.stem: How should you frame the value of a Claude-assisted drafting workflow to stakeholders?

options.A: "It completely removes any need to keep human writers anywhere on the team at all, ever again."
options.B: "It produces solid first drafts fast, which we then review and refine to keep quality high."
options.C: "It is essentially perfect, and its drafts never need any editing."
options.D: "It will do everything the team does now, only instantly and free."

questions.explanationCorrect: Honest value framing pairs the real benefit (faster first drafts, less turnaround) with the human role that preserves quality. It is credible and sustainable, unlike overclaiming.
questions.explanationDistractor: Claiming the output is perfect and never needs editing sets an expectation the tool cannot meet and erodes trust at the first necessary edit.

questions.stem: In a Claude-assisted approval workflow, who should hold accountability for the final decision?

options.A: The model itself, since it produced the underlying recommendation
options.B: No one in particular, just as long as the workflow keeps working
options.C: A designated human owner who reviews and approves the outcome
options.D: Whichever teammate happens to be the least busy on that given day

questions.explanationCorrect: Accountability must rest with a person. A designated human owner who reviews and approves keeps responsibility clear and ensures a competent check on consequential outcomes.
questions.explanationDistractor: Assigning accountability to the model is a category error; a tool cannot be answerable for a decision, so a named human must own it.

questions.stem: A hiring workflow has four steps: (1) format incoming resumes, (2) draft interview questions, (3) decide who advances, and (4) send templated scheduling emails. Which split is most appropriate?

options.A: Delegate all four of the steps entirely to Claude with no human review
options.B: Keep all four steps fully manual and do not use Claude for any of them
options.C: Delegate only the who-advances hiring decision to Claude and do all the rest by hand
options.D: Delegate formatting, drafting, and templated emails; keep the advancement decision human

questions.explanationCorrect: Delegate the well-specified, low-judgment steps (formatting, drafting, templated sends) and reserve the consequential, accountability-bearing decision, who advances, for a human.
questions.explanationDistractor: Delegating the hiring decision itself hands a high-stakes judgment about people to a tool, which is exactly the step that should stay human.

questions.stem: Your Claude-assisted workflow works well, but only you know how to run it. What most improves its long-term resilience?

options.A: Documenting the steps, prompts, and configuration so others can run it if you are away
options.B: Keep the whole workflow entirely in your own head so that you stay indispensable to the team
options.C: Delete all of your notes about it once the workflow finally works
options.D: Rebuild the entire workflow again from scratch every single month

questions.explanationCorrect: A workflow that lives only in one person's head is fragile. Documenting the steps, prompts, and configuration lets the team operate it reliably even when the original author is unavailable.
questions.explanationDistractor: Keeping it all in your head makes you a single point of failure; the workflow breaks the moment you are unavailable.

questions.stem: A stakeholder expects the new Claude workflow to be "100% accurate with no oversight." What is the best response?

options.A: Simply agree with the stakeholder's expectation outright, just to keep them satisfied and happy
options.B: Clarify that some human review remains necessary and explain where errors are most likely
options.C: Quietly remove all of the review steps to match their expectation
options.D: Tell them that output accuracy is not really something you can measure

questions.explanationCorrect: Managing expectations honestly, that review is still needed and where errors tend to occur, protects the project and the stakeholder from an unrealistic promise the tool cannot keep.
questions.explanationDistractor: Agreeing to "100% accurate with no oversight" commits to a standard no AI workflow can guarantee, setting up an inevitable, trust-damaging failure.

questions.stem: You want to show that adopting Claude improved a workflow. What is the most credible way to communicate the value?

options.A: Assert broadly and vaguely that basically everything is just "so much better now" than before
options.B: Share one dramatic success story and then generalize from that case
options.C: Compare before-and-after measures like turnaround time and rework rate, noting the human steps kept
options.D: Claim sweeping benefits that cannot really be measured or verified

questions.explanationCorrect: Credible value communication uses concrete, comparable measures (time, rework) and is honest about what still requires people. It gives stakeholders something real to evaluate.
questions.explanationDistractor: A single dramatic anecdote is not representative and can mislead; one story does not establish that the workflow reliably improved.

questions.stem: When deciding whether Claude can take an action automatically or a human must approve it first, which factor matters most?

options.A: How quickly the action itself can actually be carried out end to end
options.B: How impressive the finished automation ends up looking to others
options.C: Whether the model itself appears to handle the action confidently enough
options.D: How reversible the action is and how costly a mistake would be

questions.explanationCorrect: The key delegation test is the cost and reversibility of error: cheap, reversible actions can be automated, while costly or irreversible ones warrant human approval first.
questions.explanationDistractor: Speed is a benefit, not a safety criterion; automating an irreversible, high-cost action just because it is fast invites serious harm.

questions.stem: A colleague proposes building an elaborate automated system for a task the team does twice a year by hand in ten minutes. What is the most sensible guidance?

options.A: Match the investment to the need; a heavyweight system is overkill for a rare, quick task
options.B: Always build the most fully automated solution that is technically possible to build
options.C: Automate it thoroughly, precisely because the task is so infrequent
options.D: Add as many features as possible up front so nothing is missing later

questions.explanationCorrect: Solution design should fit the problem. For a rare, quick task, the overhead of an elaborate system outweighs any benefit; a simple manual approach (or a light assist) is more sensible.
questions.explanationDistractor: Building the most automated solution regardless of need wastes effort on a twice-a-year task and creates a system to maintain for little return.

questions.stem: You are integrating Claude into a customer-refund process. Refunds under $20 are routine; refunds over $500 are sensitive. How should you place the human checkpoint?

options.A: Require a manual human approval step for every single refund, even the tiny $2 ones
options.B: Let Claude automatically approve every single refund of any size, no matter how large
options.C: Require human approval only for the very smallest refunds
options.D: Auto-process small routine refunds and route large or unusual ones to a human

questions.explanationCorrect: Place human review where the stakes are: automate the low-risk, routine refunds and escalate the large or unusual ones. This concentrates human attention where errors are costly.
questions.explanationDistractor: Letting Claude auto-approve refunds of any size removes oversight exactly where it matters most: the large, sensitive payouts.

questions.stem: In a Claude Project, you set custom instructions that say "always write in British English and cite the source section." What is the effect?

options.A: Every chat started in that Project follows those instructions automatically
options.B: Only the very next single message that you send will actually follow those instructions
options.C: The custom instructions then apply across every single one of the Projects you own
options.D: They apply only after you repeat them again in each new chat

questions.explanationCorrect: A Project's custom instructions persist and apply to every conversation started within that Project, so shared preferences are enforced automatically without re-stating them.
questions.explanationDistractor: Custom instructions are not limited to a single message; the whole point is that they persist across every chat in the Project.

questions.stem: Your team keeps asking Claude questions about a 60-page internal handbook. What is the durable way to make that handbook available in every relevant chat?

options.A: Paste the entire 60-page internal handbook in at the start of each and every new chat
options.B: Add the handbook as a knowledge source in a Project so chats can draw on it
options.C: Ask Claude to memorize the handbook once and rely on that
options.D: Summarize the handbook from your own memory each time that it happens to come up

questions.explanationCorrect: Attaching the handbook as a Project knowledge source makes it available to every chat in the Project, so Claude can ground answers in it without anyone re-pasting the document.
questions.explanationDistractor: Asking Claude to "memorize" a document once does not work; it has no persistent memory of pasted text across separate conversations.

questions.stem: A Project's knowledge base still contains last year's pricing, and Claude keeps quoting the old prices. What is the root-cause fix?

options.A: Simply tell all of the users to mentally adjust the outdated pricing for themselves every time
options.B: Add a short note in each individual chat that manually corrects the stale price after the fact
options.C: Update the knowledge source to the current pricing so every chat inherits the correct data
options.D: Switch to a larger and more capable model whenever you happen to run those particular chats

questions.explanationCorrect: Stale configuration is a leading cause of wrong output. Updating the Project's knowledge source to current pricing fixes the problem at its root for every future chat, rather than patching each conversation.
questions.explanationDistractor: Correcting the price by hand in each chat treats the symptom repeatedly while the outdated source keeps producing the same error.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of putting durable context into a Project rather than into individual prompts?

options.A: It mainly just makes each individual prompt take longer to type out
options.B: It ends up hiding the shared context from the very people using the Project
options.C: It helps only the very first chat you create and none afterward
options.D: Every chat in the Project inherits that context, so quality and consistency improve

questions.explanationCorrect: Project context is shared by every conversation in the Project. Investing in good instructions and knowledge once raises the baseline quality and consistency of all chats that follow.
questions.explanationDistractor: Project context is not limited to the first chat; its value is precisely that it carries into every conversation in the Project.

questions.stem: Which item is best placed in a Project's custom instructions rather than typed into a single prompt?

options.A: A standing rule that all outputs use the company's four-part report structure
options.B: A quick one-time question about what today's local weather is
options.C: A throwaway request to rephrase one single sentence for you
options.D: A personal note that has nothing to do with the Project's stated purpose

questions.explanationCorrect: Durable, always-apply rules, like a standard report structure every output should follow, belong in custom instructions so they take effect automatically in every chat.
questions.explanationDistractor: A one-time weather question is transient and specific to one conversation; putting it in standing instructions would wrongly apply it to every future chat.

questions.stem: You have (1) reference documents Claude should consult and (2) rules about tone and format. In a Project, where does each belong?

options.A: Put both the reference documents and the rules into the custom instructions field
options.B: Reference documents as knowledge sources, tone and format rules as custom instructions
options.C: Put both the reference documents and the behavioral rules in as knowledge
options.D: Neither the documents nor the rules really belong in a Project at all

questions.explanationCorrect: Knowledge sources hold reference material Claude draws on; custom instructions hold standing behavioral rules like tone and format. Matching each to its slot keeps the Project organized and effective.
questions.explanationDistractor: Pasting large reference documents into the instructions field misuses it; bulky reference material belongs in knowledge sources, with instructions reserved for rules.

questions.stem: Your company just changed its refund policy, and several Projects rely on the old policy document. What should you do?

options.A: Leave the outdated documents in place; Claude will simply work out the new policy on its own
options.B: Wait until someone actually complains about a wrong policy answer
options.C: Update the policy document in the affected Projects so chats reflect the new rules
options.D: Delete all of the affected Projects entirely and then start over again from nothing

questions.explanationCorrect: Configuration must be kept current as facts change. Proactively updating the policy document in the affected Projects prevents Claude from confidently applying outdated rules.
questions.explanationDistractor: Waiting for a complaint means Claude keeps giving wrong, outdated answers in the meantime; keeping config current is a proactive maintenance task.

questions.stem: You do two very different kinds of work: legal contract review and social-media copywriting. How should you organize Projects for the best context in each?

options.A: Cram everything into one single Project so that all of the context is always available at once
options.B: Use no Projects at all and just paste the relevant context each time
options.C: Randomly assign each chat to whichever Project happens to be open
options.D: Create a separate Project for each, with its own instructions and knowledge tailored to that work

questions.explanationCorrect: Separate Projects keep each body of instructions and knowledge focused and relevant. Tailored context per Project prevents the legal rules and the copywriting rules from bleeding into the wrong chats.
questions.explanationDistractor: Cramming both kinds of work into one Project mixes unrelated instructions and knowledge, diluting the context and risking cross-contamination of guidance.

questions.stem: A new hire's Claude outputs do not match the team's house style, while veterans' outputs do. What is the most scalable fix?

options.A: Give the team a shared Project whose instructions and knowledge encode the house style, so everyone starts the same
options.B: Have the new hire shadow an experienced veteran for a full month before they are allowed to touch Claude
options.C: Ask the new hire to infer the house style on their own from past documents
options.D: Simply accept that new hires will always be off-style for their first while

questions.explanationCorrect: Encoding the house style once in a shared Project gives every team member, new or veteran, the same durable context, making consistent output the default rather than something each person recreates.
questions.explanationDistractor: Having the new hire guess the style from old documents is slow and unreliable, and it leaves the knowledge uncaptured for the next new hire.

questions.stem: What is a good practice for Project knowledge that references facts, policies, or data that change over time?

options.A: Set the knowledge once and then never actually look at it again
options.B: Review and refresh it on a regular cadence so it stays accurate
options.C: Assume that Claude itself will keep the knowledge updated automatically
options.D: Only bother to update it after some major public incident occurs

questions.explanationCorrect: Knowledge that references changeable facts drifts out of date. Reviewing and refreshing it on a regular cadence keeps every chat grounded in current information.
questions.explanationDistractor: Claude does not automatically update your uploaded knowledge sources; keeping them current is the owner's responsibility.

questions.stem: Without any reference material, Claude sometimes guesses at your product's specifications. How does a well-configured Project reduce this?

options.A: It mainly just makes Claude sound a great deal more confident even while it is still guessing
options.B: It disables Claude's ability to answer questions about the product
options.C: It supplies the real specifications as knowledge, so Claude answers from your source
options.D: It has no real effect on the accuracy of the answers either way

questions.explanationCorrect: Providing the actual specifications as Project knowledge grounds Claude's answers in your real data, reducing the guessing that leads to inaccurate claims about your product.
questions.explanationDistractor: A Project does not make guessing more confident; it replaces guessing with grounded answers by giving Claude the real reference material.

questions.stem: A Project's custom instruction reads only "be professional," yet outputs vary widely in structure and length. What would most improve consistency?

options.A: Remove the vague instruction from the Project entirely
options.B: Add several more vague, subjective adjectives, such as "good" and "nice"
options.C: Switch to a different model for each new chat in the Project
options.D: Make the instruction specific: define the structure, length, and tone you expect

questions.explanationCorrect: Vague instructions produce varied results. Specifying the concrete structure, length, and tone gives every chat a precise target, which is what drives consistency.
questions.explanationDistractor: Adding more vague adjectives compounds the ambiguity; "good" and "nice" give Claude no more concrete direction than "professional" did.

questions.stem: Different team members keep their own slightly different copies of the prompt instructions, and outputs have drifted apart. What is the best remedy?

options.A: Let every individual person simply keep refining their own separate and private version of it
options.B: Consolidate into one shared Project configuration that everyone uses as the source of truth
options.C: Email a freshly revised instruction sheet out to everyone every week
options.D: Stop giving Claude any standing instructions at all from now on

questions.explanationCorrect: Divergent private copies cause drift. A single shared Project configuration acts as the source of truth so everyone works from the same, maintained instructions and knowledge.
questions.explanationDistractor: Letting each person refine a private version is what produced the drift; it guarantees the copies keep diverging.

questions.stem: A Project's knowledge contains three versions of the same policy: last year's, a draft, and the current one. Claude sometimes cites the wrong version. What should you do?

options.A: Add a fourth, combined version of the policy just to be safe
options.B: Tell all of the users to specify the exact policy version they mean in each question
options.C: Leave all three in place, since having more documents is always better
options.D: Remove the outdated and draft versions, keeping only the current authoritative one

questions.explanationCorrect: Conflicting documents let Claude cite the wrong one. Keeping only the current, authoritative version removes the ambiguity at the source so every chat references the right policy.
questions.explanationDistractor: "More documents is always better" is false when they conflict; extra outdated versions are exactly what causes Claude to cite the wrong policy.

questions.stem: While debugging, you are about to paste a configuration file that includes a live production API key into a chat. What should you do?

options.A: Remove or redact the secret before sharing; never paste live credentials
options.B: Paste the whole config file in as-is, since doing so noticeably speeds up the debugging
options.C: Paste the file in, but ask Claude to simply ignore the embedded production key
options.D: Paste it now and then rotate the key sometime next quarter

questions.explanationCorrect: Live credentials should never be pasted into external tools. Redact or remove the secret first; asking a tool to "ignore" a key does not undo the exposure.
questions.explanationDistractor: Asking Claude to "ignore" the key does nothing to protect it; the secret has still left your controlled environment the moment it is pasted.

questions.stem: You want to analyze a spreadsheet of customers' names, addresses, and health conditions. What is the responsible first step?

options.A: Paste the spreadsheet immediately, since analysis is harmless
options.B: Check your organization's data policy and get authorization before using regulated personal data
options.C: Assume that it is perfectly fine simply because the data is only ever being summarized here
options.D: Remove just the mailing addresses and paste in all of the rest

questions.explanationCorrect: Names tied to health conditions are sensitive, regulated personal data. Responsible use requires following your organization's data policy and obtaining authorization before putting such data into any tool.
questions.explanationDistractor: Removing only the addresses still leaves names linked to health conditions, highly sensitive PII that its own governance requirements apply to.

questions.stem: A teammate suggests pasting an unreleased, confidential product roadmap into a tool that is not approved for confidential data. What is the right response?

options.A: Just go ahead and paste the whole roadmap in, since a roadmap is not really that secret anyway
options.B: Paste a "lightly edited" version of the roadmap to be a bit safer
options.C: Do not use an unapproved tool for confidential data; follow the policy on where it may go
options.D: Paste it, and then delete the chat afterward to clean it all up

questions.explanationCorrect: Confidential material should only go to tools approved for it. Understanding and following the policy on where sensitive data is allowed to flow is central to responsible use.
questions.explanationDistractor: Deleting the chat afterward does not retroactively make an unapproved destination compliant; the confidential data was already sent there.

questions.stem: Before entering any sensitive business data into an AI tool, the most important thing to understand is:

options.A: How quickly the AI tool itself tends to respond to a fairly typical everyday request from a user
options.B: How colorful and modern the tool's user interface happens to be
options.C: Whether the tool's output will be neatly formatted as a table
options.D: Where the data goes, how it may be used or retained, and whether your policy permits it

questions.explanationCorrect: Responsible use starts with data awareness: knowing where your input goes, how it may be used or retained, and whether policy allows it. That determines whether entering the data is appropriate at all.
questions.explanationDistractor: Response speed is a convenience factor, not a governance consideration; it tells you nothing about whether the data is safe or permitted to enter the tool.

questions.stem: Which of the following is clearly inappropriate to paste into a general AI chat tool?

options.A: A colleague's password and a customer's full credit-card number
options.B: A publicly available product brochure put out by the marketing team
options.C: A rough draft of a blog post you already wrote for the public website
options.D: A short list of some common English-language idioms and everyday sayings

questions.explanationCorrect: Secrets and sensitive personal financial data, passwords and full card numbers, must never be entered into a general tool. The other items are already public or non-sensitive.
questions.explanationDistractor: A publicly available brochure carries no confidentiality or privacy risk, so it is not comparable to pasting passwords or card numbers.

questions.stem: You need Claude to help spot trends in support tickets, but the tickets contain customer names and emails you do not need for the analysis. What is the best practice?

options.A: Include every single one of the customer's personal details, just to be extra thorough
options.B: Remove or anonymize the personal details you do not need before sending the data
options.C: Include the customer emails, but strip out the customer names
options.D: Send absolutely everything over to the tool and just hope that none of it is retained

questions.explanationCorrect: Data minimization means sharing only what the task requires. Stripping or anonymizing personal details you do not need for trend analysis reduces exposure while still enabling the work.
questions.explanationDistractor: Keeping the emails but dropping the names still transmits personal contact data that the trend analysis does not require.

questions.stem: A user asks Claude to help them access an ex-partner's private accounts without permission. As a responsible operator, what is the right stance?

options.A: Help them out, since the user did ask for it quite politely
options.B: Go ahead and help them, as long as doing so is technically feasible in the first place
options.C: Decline; this is unauthorized access to someone else's private accounts, however it is framed
options.D: Help, but attach a disclaimer about using the access responsibly

questions.explanationCorrect: Responsible use includes refusing tasks that facilitate harm or unauthorized access to others' private data. Neither politeness nor technical feasibility makes the request acceptable.
questions.explanationDistractor: Adding a disclaimer does not change the nature of the act; assisting unauthorized access to someone's private accounts is inappropriate regardless of a caveat.

questions.stem: Your company classifies data as Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted. Before pasting a document into an AI tool, the classification matters because:

options.A: A document with a higher data classification reliably produces noticeably better model answers
options.B: The classification really only affects the tool's file-size limits
options.C: The color of the label itself changes how the model behaves
options.D: It tells you the handling rules: some classes may not be entered into certain tools at all

questions.explanationCorrect: Data classification drives handling requirements. Knowing a document's class tells you whether, and in which tools, it may be used, which is the governance question that comes before any prompt.
questions.explanationDistractor: Classification is about handling rules and permitted destinations, not file-size limits; it governs whether the data may be entered at all.

questions.stem: A clinic wants to use a general consumer AI tool to summarize identifiable patient records. Before doing so, the key governance question is:

options.A: Whether that use is permitted under applicable health-privacy rules and the tool's approved handling
options.B: Whether each of the generated summaries will come in under 200 words
options.C: Whether the clinic's own staff would tend to prefer neat bullet points or flowing narrative prose
options.D: Whether the tool offers a dark mode for the late-night shifts

questions.explanationCorrect: Identifiable patient records are protected health information. The governing question is whether the intended use complies with health-privacy rules and the tool's approved handling, not stylistic preferences.
questions.explanationDistractor: The length or formatting of the summaries is irrelevant to whether it is lawful and permitted to process identifiable patient data in that tool.

questions.stem: Before forwarding a Claude-generated report to an external partner, you should:

options.A: Just send the report straight to the partner, since it was generated internally in the first place
options.B: Review it to ensure no confidential or personal internal data was carried into the output
options.C: Only check the report over carefully for any spelling mistakes
options.D: Assume Claude already removed anything sensitive automatically

questions.explanationCorrect: Outputs can inadvertently include sensitive details drawn from your inputs. Reviewing before external sharing prevents leaking confidential or personal information outside the organization.
questions.explanationDistractor: Claude does not automatically know which of your internal details are confidential; assuming it stripped them is unsafe before an external send.

questions.stem: An employee starts using a personal, unvetted AI account for work involving company data because it is convenient. What is the governance concern?

options.A: There really is no concern here; convenience is honestly all that truly matters
options.B: Only that the personal account might turn out to be a little slower
options.C: Company data may flow through an unapproved tool, outside the organization's controls
options.D: Only that the tool's fonts and colors happen to look a bit different

questions.explanationCorrect: Using unapproved, personal tools for company data routes sensitive information outside sanctioned controls, data-handling agreements, and oversight, a core governance risk regardless of convenience.
questions.explanationDistractor: Speed is not the issue; the real concern is company data leaving approved, governed channels through an unvetted personal account.

questions.stem: Which principle best guides how much data to include when prompting with real business information?

options.A: Include only the data necessary for the task, and no more
options.B: Always include the maximum data available, for the fullest context
options.C: Include everything and let Claude decide what it should ignore
options.D: Include some extra unrelated data as a way to test the model

questions.explanationCorrect: Data minimization, sharing only what the task needs, limits exposure of sensitive information and is a foundational responsible-use practice.
questions.explanationDistractor: Dumping the maximum available data needlessly exposes sensitive information that the task never required, increasing risk with no benefit.

questions.stem: Two AI tools are available. Tool X is approved by your company with a data agreement in place; Tool Y is a random free site with unknown data practices. For confidential work, which should you use and why?

options.A: Tool Y, purely on the grounds that a free tool is simply cheaper for the whole team to keep using
options.B: Either one of the two tools; honestly it makes no real difference for confidential data
options.C: Tool X, because its approved status and data agreement govern how your data is handled
options.D: Whichever of the two tools happens to load faster in your browser

questions.explanationCorrect: For confidential work, the approved tool with a known data agreement is the responsible choice; you understand and have assurances about where the data goes and how it is handled.
questions.explanationDistractor: A free site with unknown data practices offers no assurances about retention or use, making it unsuitable for confidential data regardless of cost.

questions.stem: An organization wants a simple rule for employees about sensitive data and AI tools. Which rule is soundest?

options.A: "Move fast: any tool is fine as long as it helps you hit deadlines, and sort out the data questions later."
options.B: "Never use AI tools for any work at all; the risk of data exposure always outweighs any possible benefit."
options.C: "Use whatever tool you happen to like even for sensitive data, so long as you delete the conversation afterward to erase the exposure."
options.D: "Use only approved tools, follow the data-classification policy, and never enter secrets or regulated personal data without authorization."

questions.explanationCorrect: A sound rule combines approved tools, adherence to data classification, and a clear prohibition on entering secrets or regulated personal data without authorization, covering the main governance risks concisely.
questions.explanationDistractor: Deleting the chat afterward (option C) does not reverse the exposure; the sensitive data has already left your controlled environment, so "delete later" is not real protection.

questions.stem: Claude's answers to your question are consistently generic and could apply to any company. What is the most likely root cause and fix?

options.A: The prompt lacks specific context; add the concrete details unique to your situation
options.B: The underlying model itself must be fundamentally broken, so you should go file a bug report
options.C: You simply need to go ahead and ask it the exact same question several more times over
options.D: The maximum output length setting is turned up far too high

questions.explanationCorrect: Generic output usually traces back to a generic, context-poor prompt. Supplying the specifics of your situation is the durable fix that makes answers relevant.
questions.explanationDistractor: Repeating the same context-free question just yields more generic answers; the missing ingredient is the specific context, not repetition.

questions.stem: You have clearly described the output format three times and Claude still gets the layout slightly wrong. What is the most effective durable fix?

options.A: Describe the desired format a fourth time, only more emphatically
options.B: Provide a concrete example of the exact output layout you want
options.C: Give up on it and simply reformat the output by hand every single time
options.D: Switch over to a completely different task altogether instead of this one

questions.explanationCorrect: When descriptions of a format keep missing, a worked example demonstrates the target directly. It is usually the durable fix that repeated re-describing is not.
questions.explanationDistractor: Reformatting by hand every time treats the symptom forever; an example fixes the root cause so Claude produces the right layout itself.

questions.stem: A high-volume, simple text-cleanup job is running slowly and costing more than expected on your largest model. What is the root-cause fix?

options.A: Add quite a few more detailed instructions on top of the existing cleanup prompt
options.B: Run the whole job twice over just to be sure of the result
options.C: Switch the job to a smaller, faster model suited to simple high-volume work
options.D: Increase the maximum output length that is allowed for each and every response
